# Implement block: Pinch to Summarize (SwiftUI)

You are adding the "Pinch to Summarize" block from Native Cook to the user's iOS app. The block already exists as working SwiftUI code. Your job is to bring it into this project faithfully, not to write a new one that looks similar.

## The block

A long-form review in an invented reading app, with a masthead, a dark header panel, a serif headline and a duotone photo. Pinch the article and the summary is visibly made from it: while the fingers close, the rest of the page washes out and four key sentences get a lavender highlighter sweep, locking in one by one with a tick; a small label under the page shows how deep the summary will be (Key points, Brief or TL;DR, deeper pinch, shorter summary). Let go and the page waits, still readable, while the picked sentences pulse in turn (“Summarizing for you…” if it takes a moment). Then each sentence lifts off the page as a chip and flies on a curved path into the summary line it became, while the page settles into a small card at the top of a drifting blue-to-pink gradient. The summary is a lead, entity chips (tap one to light its words) and icon-led points with source marks; the price rolls in and the review meter fills to 4 of 5. The card shows how far you had read, and the footer reads “You read 50% · 14 min → 40 s” with rolling numbers. Tap a point to see its sentence in the article, flashed; pinch out, tap the card or the close button and the chips fly home. Long-press the summary to lift it as a card with Copy summary and Share. The article keeps an opaque band under the status bar, so nothing scrolls over the clock.

**Motion.** Progress p = (1 − scale) / 0.5 while pinching in and 1 − (scale − 1) / 0.8 while pinching out, with Apple's rubber band (0.55) past either end; the page scales from 1 towards 0.55 of the screen, follows the focal point ×0.6 and crops late (p^2.2) so the article stays whole. Highlighter: g = p / 0.45, sentence i sweeps left to right over its fifth and locks at g = 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 (selection haptic and an 180 ms pop each); the veil over the rest reaches 62 %. Depth: Brief past p 0.62, TL;DR past 0.85 (±0.03 hysteresis, selection haptic, lens spring 300 ms, damping ratio 0.8). Release commits on momentum projection past p 0.32 (soft haptic); unlocked sentences finish their sweep at 150 ms each and the page springs (400 ms, damping ratio 0.8, the finger's velocity handed over) to a hold at p 0.42–0.6. The answer takes 1.1 s; after 300 ms the sentences pulse in turn, 200 ms each. Distill: chips leave 60 ms apart and travel 420 ms on bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1) along a quadratic path bowed 28 pt + 14 % of the drop, scaling to their line's width, ink to white over 20–50 %, the marker fading over 15–55 %, cross-fading into the line over 55–100 %; a sentence the depth leaves out dissolves in place. The page springs to the card (300 ms, damping ratio 0.8) while its scroll rewinds to the top in 600 ms; titles and discs rise in once their chip has landed (300 ms, 6 pt rise, ease-out); the success haptic and a bloom ring come with the last landing. Entity chips rise 40 ms apart, 220 ms on bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1); the price rolls 520 ms; meter segments fill 40 ms apart, 180 ms each; the reading time and share read roll 600 ms on the same curve; the progress bar fills over 600 ms once the card has settled. Way back: chips fly home on the same curve, the one at the front of the travel first (a sentence that melted into another line reappears in place), while the page springs open (400 ms, damping ratio 1, never past the full page) and scrolls to where the reader was (or to the tapped point's sentence, which flashes, 200 ms on bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1)); highlights fade over 400 ms after 400 ms. Share card: long-press 350 ms, scale 1.03 and a shadow on a 300 ms spring (damping ratio 0.8), actions rise 12 pt; a tap away drops it in 150 ms. Presses answer at once: scale 0.97, 150 ms down and 100 ms back on bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1), and a summary point shows a soft backing; nothing under a two-finger pinch lights up or lifts. A gesture that catches the chips mid-flight fades them where they are (120 ms) while their sentences come back on the page. Autoplay: a 10 s loop (LOOP_MS 10000) of a read scroll (0.4 to 1.5 s), scripted fingers on the same worklets (pinch in 1.7 to 2.6 s to scale 0.76, the summary arriving after the 1.1 s think; pinch out 6.8 to 7.65 s to 1.8) and a scroll back to the top (8.3 to 9.4 s); a touch stops it and it resumes 2 s after the last touch; under Reduce Motion there is no autoplay. Reduce Motion: no flight, scale or drift; highlights appear whole, the page and summary cross-fade (180 ms), numbers jump, presses dim instead of scaling and a pinch out dims the summary.

## Reference source

The block is built and running in the Native Cook source repository. Each link below is a file on GitHub. To read one as plain text, replace `https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/` with `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/` in its address.

## Your instructions

_Anything specific to this app goes here: where the block should appear, what to rename, what to change. Left empty, integrate the block as it is._

## How to work

Work like an experienced iOS engineer joining an existing project: learn the app first, read only what you need, decide early how the block fits, then integrate it with as little disruption as possible. Take the steps in order.

**Done means** the block is reachable in the user's app and behaves like the reference in the iOS Simulator or on a device. A SwiftUI preview is useful while you work, but it is not the proof: build and run the app.

**Fidelity.** Bring over the real implementation. Keep its structure, colours, sizes, timings and curves. Change only what this project requires and what "Your instructions" ask for.

If you already learned this project earlier in the conversation, reuse what you know and skip step 2. Learn it again only if the project changed or something you need is missing.

### 1. Check where you are

- You need the project's files and a terminal. If this prompt was pasted into a chat that has neither, stop and say so: it has to be run by a coding agent opened on the project.
- Confirm the project is an iOS app built with Xcode (an `.xcodeproj`, an `.xcworkspace` or a Swift package with an app target). If it is something else, stop, say what you found, and do not create a new app inside it unless the instructions ask for one.

### 2. Learn the host app

- The app target, its deployment target and its Swift version.
- SwiftUI, UIKit or both, and how a screen is shown today: `NavigationStack`, a coordinator, a tab bar, a storyboard.
- How files join the target: a folder the project synchronises, or a file list in the project that you have to extend.
- Conventions: folder layout, naming, where colours, fonts and assets live.
- Type names the app already uses, so the block's types do not collide with them.

### 3. Read the block

- Swift files in a module do not import each other, so the demo alone will not lead you to the rest. The list above names every file of the block: read them all.
- The demo is how the source repository shows the block. Bring over what the demo shows, not the repository's gallery. Anything listed under "Used by the demo only" stays behind.
- Read the block's initialiser and its defaults. The demo may switch on an option that makes the block play by itself for a recording (for example `autoPlay`). Keep the option; leave it off in the user's app unless asked.

### 4. Decide the fit

- The source app targets iOS 17. If the host targets an older system, check each API the block uses and tell the user what would have to change before you lower anything. Do not raise the host's deployment target without asking.
- If a type or function name of the block already exists in the app, rename the block's one, in every file that uses it, and say that you did.
- Shared helpers: copy the ones the block uses next to it, or fold them into the block's files. Do not copy helpers it never calls.
- In a UIKit app, show the block through a `UIHostingController`.

### 5. Bring it in

- Add the block's files to the app target, keeping their names.
- Copy its asset catalogs, loose resources and fonts, and check that the names the code asks for match the names in the bundle: a wrong name compiles and then shows nothing.
- A `.metal` file has to be compiled into the same target as the code that calls its function.
- Keep reduced-motion handling, haptics and accessibility labels as they are in the source.
- Mount the block where the instructions say. With no instructions, add a screen named after the block and make it reachable the way the app's other screens are.

### 6. Run it

- Build the app target for a simulator with `xcodebuild` or the project's own script, and fix every error and new warning the block introduced.
- Run it and use the block: every state, every gesture, light and dark appearance if the block follows them, and once with Reduce Motion on.
- If the build or the simulator fails for a reason outside the block, report the error and ask how to continue.

### 7. Report

- Files added and changed, and anything renamed to avoid a collision.
- How to reach the block in the app.
- Anything that differs from the reference, and why.
